claim: Animals can learn causal relationships between pairs of stimuli separated in time and this ability depends on the hippocampus.
source: Animals can learn causal relationships between pairs of stimuli separated in time and this ability depends on the hippocampus.
evidence: This is a general statement about animal learning that draws from established scientific knowledge in the field.

claim: Area CA1 cells converge to time-locked firing sequences that bridge the two stimuli paired during training.
source: Here, we show that area CA1 cells converge to time-locked firing sequences that bridge the two stimuli paired during training, and this phenomenon is coupled to a reorganization of network correlations.
evidence: This is a primary finding of the study supported by experimental data from two-photon calcium imaging.

claim: The emergence of time-locked firing sequences is coupled to a reorganization of network correlations.
source: Here, we show that area CA1 cells converge to time-locked firing sequences that bridge the two stimuli paired during training, and this phenomenon is coupled to a reorganization of network correlations.
evidence: This is a primary finding supported by experimental measurements of spontaneous activity correlations.

claim: Co-time-tuned neurons exhibit enhanced spontaneous activity correlations that increase just prior to learning.
source: Using two-photon calcium imaging of mouse hippocampal neurons we find that co-time-tuned neurons exhibit enhanced spontaneous activity correlations that increase just prior to learning.
evidence: This is a finding from the study supported by correlation analysis of calcium imaging data.

claim: Time-tuned cells are not spatially organized.
source: While time-tuned cells are not spatially organized, spontaneously correlated cells do fall into distinct spatial clusters that change as a result of learning.
evidence: This is supported by spatial analysis of cell locations within the imaged fields of view.

claim: Spontaneously correlated cells fall into distinct spatial clusters that change as a result of learning.
source: While time-tuned cells are not spatially organized, spontaneously correlated cells do fall into distinct spatial clusters that change as a result of learning.
evidence: This is a finding from the study supported by clustering analysis and spatial mapping of neurons.

claim: The spatial re-organization of correlation clusters reflects global network connectivity changes that are responsible for the emergence of sequentially-timed activity.
source: We propose that the spatial re-organization of correlation clusters reflects global network connectivity changes that are responsible for the emergence of the sequentially-timed activity of cell-groups underlying the learned behavior.
evidence: This is a proposed interpretation of the experimental findings.

claim: Hebbian plasticity is the neural mechanism for the association of two co-occurring stimuli.
source: Much evidence points to Hebbian plasticity as the neural mechanism for the association of two co-occurring stimuli (Bliss and Collingridge, 1993; Morris, 2003).
evidence: This is supported by citations to previous research.

claim: Hebbian plasticity alone is not sufficient to account for learning when two stimuli are separated in time by more than 100 ms.
source: However, this mechanism alone is not sufficient to account for learning under conditions where the two stimuli are separated in time by more than 100 ms (Levy and Steward, 1983), as has been commonly observed (Solomon et al., 1986; Baeg et al., 2003).
evidence: This is supported by citations to previous research.

claim: The hippocampus is required for learning the trace conditioning task.
source: Lesion studies have shown that the hippocampus is required for learning the trace conditioning task, but not a related delay conditioning task, where the CS and US overlap in time (Büchel et al., 1999; Tseng et al., 2004).
evidence: This is supported by citations to lesion studies.

claim: The hippocampus is not required for learning the delay conditioning task where the CS and US overlap in time.
source: Lesion studies have shown that the hippocampus is required for learning the trace conditioning task, but not a related delay conditioning task, where the CS and US overlap in time (Büchel et al., 1999; Tseng et al., 2004).
evidence: This is supported by citations to lesion studies.

claim: Sequential activity in hippocampal CA1 cells has been observed in temporal memory tasks.
source: Sequential activity in hippocampal CA1 cells has been seen previously, albeit in some very different behavioral contexts, including temporal memory tasks (Louie and Wilson, 2001; Pastalkova et al., 2008; Gill et al., 2011).
evidence: This is supported by citations to previous research.

claim: Hippocampal CA1 neurons show stimulus-triggered, time-locked sequences in stimulus-retention tasks.
source: Here too, hippocampal CA1 neurons were observed to be active in stimulus-triggered, time-locked sequences (MacDonald et al., 2011; Naya and Suzuki, 2011; Kraus et al., 2013; MacDonald et al., 2013).
evidence: This is supported by citations to previous research.

claim: Hippocampal CA1 cells adopt sequential activity patterns when subjects are placed in a behavioral context requiring the bridging of temporally separated stimuli.
source: It is increasingly clear that hippocampal CA1 cells adopt sequential activity patterns when subjects are placed in a behavioral context requiring the bridging of temporally separated stimuli.
evidence: This is a synthesis of findings from multiple cited studies.

claim: The time course and mechanism of the emergence of sequentially timed activity is entirely unknown.
source: However, in all the studies where this has been observed, only well-trained subjects were used, leaving the time course and mechanism of the emergence of sequentially timed activity entirely unknown.
evidence: This is an inference based on the limitations of previous studies.

claim: Functional connectivity can be measured by correlations between neuronal activity in the absence of stimulus presentation.
source: Functional connectivity, as measured by correlations between neuronal activity in the absence of stimulus presentation, is one way to monitor such network changes (Ts'o et al., 1986; Bair et al., 2001; Fujisawa et al., 2008).
evidence: This is supported by citations to previous research.

claim: Changes in spontaneous activity correlations indicate learning-related circuit plasticity.
source: In a study using two photon calcium imaging of motor cortex pyramidal neuron activity, changes in spontaneous activity correlations have been inferred to indicate learning-related circuit plasticity (Komiyama et al., 2010).
evidence: This is supported by citation to previous research.

claim: Correlations between pairs of place cells increased with increasing exposure to a novel environment.
source: In another study where rats were exploring a novel track, correlations between pairs of place cells increased with increasing exposure to the novel environment (Cheng and Frank, 2008; Dragoi and Tonegawa, 2013).
evidence: This is supported by citations to previous research.

claim: Nine of 18 trace conditioned mice learned the association to criterion.
source: 9 of 18 trace conditioned mice had performance scores higher than those of the pseudo-conditioned mice.
evidence: This is a direct result from the behavioral experiments.

claim: The mean learning trial across learner mice was trial 26.
source: The mean of the individual learning trials was 26 ± 5 (mean ± SD, n = 9 learners; for six of these learner mice, imaging data was also acquired, Video 1 shows high-speed video of mouse blinks before and after learning).
evidence: This is a statistical result from the behavioral analysis.

claim: Trace conditioned mice had significantly higher performance scores than pseudo-conditioned mice.
source: These pseudo-conditioned mice did not demonstrate an increase in blink amplitude or duration (performance scores, trace = 8.74 ± 2.73, pseudo = 1.96 ± 0.44, mean ± standard error of the mean (SEM); Figure 1E,F, two-sample t test, p=0.012).
evidence: This is supported by statistical comparison of behavioral data shown in Figure 1E,F.

claim: The mean response width of CA1 cells was 120 ms ± 81 ms.
source: The mean response width measured in this manner was found to be 120 ms ± 81 ms (mean ± SD, n = 542 cells, Figure 2B).
evidence: This is a direct measurement from calcium imaging data shown in Figure 2B.

claim: Only 0.5% of cells had response widths greater than 600 ms.
source: Only three cells (∼0.5%, of all cells) had response widths greater than 600 ms, the length of the period from tone-onset to puff-onset.
evidence: This is a statistical result from the calcium imaging data analysis.

claim: Sustained cell activation is not the mechanism used by the hippocampus to maintain a stimulus representation.
source: Based on this analysis, we concluded that sustained cell activation is not the mechanism used by the hippocampus to maintain a stimulus representation.
evidence: This is a conclusion drawn from the response width analysis.

claim: Post learning, area CA1 cells had activity peaks at fixed time-points relative to tone onset, seen consistently across multiple trials.
source: Post learning, however, we observed that area CA1 cells had activity peaks at fixed time-points relative to tone onset, seen consistently across multiple trials (Figure 2C, right panel).
evidence: This is a finding from the calcium imaging data shown in Figure 2C.

claim: Small groups of cells firing at each time-point tiled the entire interval of interest.
source: We rank ordered cells based on the timings of their activity peaks and found that small groups of cells firing at each time-point, tiled the entire interval of interest (Figure 2D).
evidence: This is a finding from the analysis of calcium imaging data shown in Figure 2D.

claim: Timings of peak activity of area CA1 cells changed during training.
source: This indicated that timings of peak activity of area CA1 cells, relative to the onset of tone stimulus, changed during training.
evidence: This is a conclusion drawn from comparing pre-training and post-training activity patterns.

claim: Reliability scores for area CA1 cells in mice that learned the task were significantly higher than for pseudo-conditioned mice, non-learners, and spontaneous activity data.
source: Reliability scores for area CA1 cells in mice that learned the task (n = 542 cells from 6 mice), were significantly higher than reliability scores for neurons from pseudo-conditioned mice (n = 498 cells from 6 mice), non-learners (n = 612 cells from 8 mice) and for spontaneous activity data from the trace learners (trace = 3.12 ± 0.20, pseudo = 1.35 ± 0.08, spontaneous = 0.84 ± 0.07, non- learners = 1.72 ± 0.13; mean ± SEM; ANOVA followed by h.s.d., p<0.01; Figure 3D).
evidence: This is a statistical result from the reliability score analysis shown in Figure 3D.

claim: 44% of neurons from trace learners had reliability scores close to 1, displaying no time-locked activity.
source: On plotting the distribution of all reliability scores obtained for cells from trace learners, we found that 44% of neurons had reliability scores close to 1, that is they displayed no time-locked activity (Figure 3—figure supplement 1B).
evidence: This is a statistical result from the distribution analysis shown in Figure 3—figure supplement 1B.

claim: Reliability scores for neurons from trace learners increased over the training session.
source: We found that the reliability scores for neurons from trace learners increased over the training session (Figure 3E) and that this increase was significantly greater than that seen in pseudo-conditioned mice or in spontaneous activity data from trace conditioned mice (Figure 3F, ANOVA followed by Tukey–Kramer h.s.d., p<0.01).
evidence: This is a finding from the time-course analysis shown in Figures 3E and 3F.

claim: The first trial bin where the increase in reliability scores is seen is for trials 21–25, which coincides with the mean behavioral learning trial.
source: Interestingly, the first trial bin where the increase in reliability scores is seen is for trials 21–25. This coincides well with the mean behavioral learning trial (24 ± 1 for imaged mice, 26 ± 2 for all mice mean ± SEM).
evidence: This is a comparison of timing between reliability score increases and behavioral learning.

claim: Most cells do not increase their response probability with training.
source: On average, no training-related increases in local reliability score were detectable. This indicates that most cells do not increase their response probability with training.
evidence: This is a conclusion from the local reliability score analysis.

claim: Reliability scores increase as learning progresses mainly due to changes in the peak-timings of cell activity during learning.
source: Hence, we concluded that reliability scores increase as learning progresses and that this increase is mainly due to changes in the peak-timings of cell activity during learning.
evidence: This is a conclusion drawn from multiple analyses of peak timing changes.

claim: The distribution of peak response times was non-uniform before training and early in training, but became more uniform after learning.
source: The distribution was clearly non-uniform both before (χ2 goodness of fit test with uniform expected distribution; χ2 = 69.14, p<10−4, Figure 3G) as well as at an early stage of trace conditioning (χ2 = 61.92, p<10−4, Figure 3H). However, for the group of trials after the learning trial, the distribution was much closer to a uniform distribution (χ2 = 20.53, p=0.015, Figure 3I).
evidence: This is a statistical result from the distribution analysis shown in Figures 3G, 3H, and 3I.

claim: Time-decoder prediction accuracy scores for trace learners were significantly higher than for pseudo-conditioned mice, spontaneous activity data, and non-learners.
source: The time-decoder prediction accuracy scores (normalized to decoder accuracy for control, time-shuffled data) for data from trace learners were significantly higher than those for data from pseudo-conditioned mice, spontaneous activity data from trace learners and data from non-learners (trace = 2.28 ± 0.27, pseudo = 1.26 ± 0.10, spontaneous = 1.37 ± 0.06, non-learners = 1.59 ± 0.16, mean ± SEM; ANOVA, followed by Tukey Kramer h.s.d., p<0.01; Figure 3J).
evidence: This is a statistical result from the time-decoder analysis shown in Figure 3J.

claim: Neurons sharing time-tuning were not spatially clustered together.
source: The mean pair-wise distance between neurons sharing time-tuning was not significantly different from the mean distance between random pairs of neurons, that is neurons sharing time-tuning were not spatially clustered together (mean ± SEM distance for same time-tuning 71.27 ± 1.53 µm, random 70.89 ± 0.62 µm; Figure 3—figure supplement 1G,H; two-sample t test p=0.73).
evidence: This is a statistical result from the spatial analysis shown in Figure 3—figure supplement 1G,H.

claim: Mean noise correlation increased during the training session for trace conditioned learners, with a peak at trial bin 16-20.
source: Interestingly, for trace conditioned learners, mean NC increased during the training session, with a peak at trial bin 16-20 (19 ± 2, mean ± SEM).
evidence: This is a finding from the noise correlation analysis over the training session.

claim: The peak in noise correlation precedes the peak in time-tuning and the averaged learning trial.
source: This peak precedes the peak in time-tuning (trial bin 21–25, Figure 3E) and the averaged learning trial (24 ± 1 for imaged mice, trial 26 ± 2, for all mice; mean ± SEM).
evidence: This is a comparison of timing between different measures across the training session.

claim: Noise correlation for cell-pairs with the same activity peak timing was significantly higher than for random cell-pairs.
source: Furthermore, the NC calculated for cell-pairs where both cells had the same activity peak timing was significantly higher than for random cell-pairs (same time-tuning = 0.22 ± 0.01, random pairs = 0.14 ± 0.01 (mean ± SEM), ANOVA followed by Tukey–Kramer h.s.d., p<0.01, n = 56 peak-timing points with an average of 25 cell-pairs in each group; Figure 4B).
evidence: This is a statistical result from the noise correlation analysis shown in Figure 4B.

claim: Towards the end of the session, noise correlation for neurons sharing the same peak times remained significantly higher than for randomly chosen cell pairs.
source: Towards the end of the session, NC declined, although, even at this stage, NC for neurons sharing the same peak times remained significantly higher than for randomly chosen cell pairs (same PT = 0.16 ± 0.01, random pairs = 0.10 ± 0.01; mean ± SEM; ANOVA followed by Tukey–Kramer h.s.d., p<0.01; Figure 4B).
evidence: This is a statistical result from the noise correlation analysis shown in Figure 4B.

claim: Cells from pseudo-conditioned mice showed no increase in noise correlation.
source: Cells from pseudo-conditioned mice showed no such increase in NC (same PT = 0.13 ± 0.02, random pairs = 0.12 ± 0.01; mean ± SEM; ANOVA followed by Tukey–Kramer h.s.d., p>0.01; n = 48 time-tuning points with an average of 25 cell-pairs in each; Figure 4B).
evidence: This is a statistical result from the noise correlation analysis shown in Figure 4B.

claim: Neurons with high reliability scores had significantly higher noise correlations than neurons with low reliability scores.
source: Neurons with high reliability scores had significantly higher noise correlations than neurons with low reliability scores (Figure 4—figure supplement 1B; high RS 0.24 ± 0.03, low RS 0.14 ± 0.02; mean ± SEM; * indicates p<0.01, two sample t test).
evidence: This is a statistical result from the analysis shown in Figure 4—figure supplement 1B.

claim: Activity sequences seen during the stimulus period were not re-capitulated during spontaneous activity.
source: Correlations for peak-timing offset traces were not significantly different from those for randomly offset traces (Figure 4—figure supplement 1C; peak-time offset 0.048 ± 0.0012, random offset 0.047 ± 0.0009, means ± SE; two sample t test, p=0.71).
evidence: This is a statistical result from the analysis shown in Figure 4—figure supplement 1C.

claim: Neurons clustered into distinct groups with higher within-cluster noise correlation than across-cluster noise correlation.
source: We observed that neurons clustered into distinct groups. As expected, within-cluster NC was higher than across cluster NC (Figure 5B,D, two-sample t test, p<10−4).
evidence: This is a statistical result from the clustering analysis shown in Figures 5B and 5D.

claim: Neurons belonging to the same correlation cluster were spatially clustered within the imaged fields of view.
source: Interestingly, in contrast to the groups of neurons sharing the same activity peak-timings (Figure 3—figure supplement 1G,H), neurons belonging to the same correlation cluster were spatially clustered within the imaged fields of view (examples of peak-timing groups and correlation clusters are shown in Figure 5E).
evidence: This is a finding from the spatial analysis shown in Figure 5E.

claim: The mean distance between neuron centroids for pairs of neurons belonging to the same cluster was significantly lower than for pairs from different clusters.
source: The mean distance between neuron centroids for pairs of neurons belonging to the same cluster was significantly lower than for pairs of neurons taken from different clusters (intra-cluster = 72.10 ± 1.00 µm, n = 1694 pairs, inter-cluster = 106.79 ± 0.90 µm, n = 3418 pairs, mean ± SEM; two-sample t test p<10−4, Figure 5F).
evidence: This is a statistical result from the spatial analysis shown in Figure 5F.

claim: Noise correlation and cell-cell distance were significantly, inversely correlated.
source: Furthermore, NC and cell–cell distance were also found to be significantly, inversely correlated (correlation coefficient = −0.178, p<10−4, n = 24,522 cell pairs; Figure 5—figure supplement 1A).
evidence: This is a statistical result from the correlation analysis shown in Figure 5—figure supplement 1A.

claim: Cell-groupings changed drastically during the trace conditioning session.
source: In contrast, cell-groupings changed drastically during the trace conditioning session (Figure 6A,C), and were significantly less stable than those in the pre-training datasets.
evidence: This is a finding from the cluster similarity analysis shown in Figures 6A and 6C.

claim: For pseudo-conditioned mice, cell groupings were reliable throughout the training session datasets.
source: For pseudo-conditioned mice, cell groupings were reliable throughout the training session datasets (ANOVA followed by Tukey Kramer h.s.d., p<0.01; Figure 6B,C).
evidence: This is a statistical result from the cluster similarity analysis shown in Figures 6B and 6C.

claim: Spatially organized, correlated cell-clusters exist prior to and during learning.
source: Thus, spatially organized, correlated cell-clusters exist prior to and during learning.
evidence: This is a conclusion drawn from the clustering and spatial analyses.

claim: Correlated cell-groups remain stable in the absence of training but undergo continuing re-organization during the process of learning the trace conditioning task.
source: These correlated cell-groups remain stable in the absence of training, but undergo continuing re-organization during the process of learning the trace conditioning task.
evidence: This is a conclusion drawn from comparing trace and pseudo-conditioned mice.

claim: During trace eyeblink conditioning, groups of area CA1 neurons progressively began to fire in sequences that spanned the interval from tone onset to 200 ms after the puff.
source: We showed that, during trace eyeblink conditioning, groups of area CA1 neurons progressively began to fire in sequences that spanned the interval from tone onset to 200 ms after the puff (figures 2D, 3D,E).
evidence: This is a summary of findings from the calcium imaging data shown in the referenced figures.

claim: The emergence of activity sequences became prominent at the same trial in the session at which mice learned the association.
source: This phenomenon became prominent at the same trial in the session at which mice learned the association (Figure 1G).
evidence: This is a finding from comparing the timing of neural and behavioral changes shown in Figure 1G.

claim: The emergence of activity sequences and learning were closely preceded by a transient increase in noise-correlations.
source: The emergence of activity sequences and learning were closely preceded by a transient increase in noise-correlations, and was accompanied by modifications to spatially organized clustering of correlated neurons (Figure 4A,B, 5F, 6A–C).
evidence: This is a summary of findings from the noise correlation and clustering analyses shown in the referenced figures.

claim: Neurons related to sequential activity were not spatially organized within the hippocampus.
source: As has been seen before in the context of place cells, we found that neurons related to sequential activity were not spatially organized within the hippocampus (Dombeck et al., 2010; Figure 3—figure supplement 1F,G).
evidence: This is a finding from the spatial analysis shown in Figure 3—figure supplement 1F,G, consistent with previous research.

claim: The transient, global increase in noise correlation may arise from a network-wide increase in synaptic weights during learning.
source: The transient, global increase in NC may arise from a network-wide increase in synaptic weights during learning, and the subsequent decline may reflect weakening of mean synaptic weights due to synaptic re-normalization (schematic in Figure 7B).
evidence: This is a proposed interpretation of the noise correlation findings.

claim: The subsequent decline in noise correlation may reflect weakening of mean synaptic weights due to synaptic re-normalization.
source: The transient, global increase in NC may arise from a network-wide increase in synaptic weights during learning, and the subsequent decline may reflect weakening of mean synaptic weights due to synaptic re-normalization (schematic in Figure 7B).
evidence: This is a proposed interpretation of the noise correlation findings.

claim: Area CA1 cells receive spatially segregated input from bundles of area CA3 cells.
source: This might indicate that area CA1 cells receive spatially segregated input from bundles of area CA3 cells. This is borne out by the observation of spatially segregated connectivity from CA3 to CA1 cells in hippocampal slices (Brivanlou et al., 2004).
evidence: This is an interpretation supported by citation to previous research.

claim: During learning, area CA1 cells enter a dynamic state where neurons change from one spatially-organized, correlated grouping to another.
source: Importantly, we observed that these spatially segregated clusters changed only during learning, while in pseudo-conditioned mice and in data collected prior to training, NC clusters remained relatively constant (Figure 6C). This indicates that during learning, area CA1 cells (and probably also, by extension, CA3 cells) enter a dynamic state, where neurons change from one spatially-organized, correlated grouping to another (schematic in Figure 7C).
evidence: This is a conclusion drawn from the cluster reorganization findings shown in Figure 6C.

claim: Fluctuating spatial groupings reflect network changes that underlie the emergence of spatially un-organized, behavior-related sequentially timed activity.
source: In our view, these fluctuating, spatial groupings reflect network changes that underlie the emergence of spatially un-organized, behavior-related sequentially timed activity.
evidence: This is a proposed interpretation of the findings.

claim: All experimental procedures were approved by the National Centre for Biological Sciences Institutional Animal Ethics Committee.
source: All experimental procedures were approved by the National Centre for Biological Sciences Institutional Animal Ethics Committee (Protocol number USB–19–1/2011), in accordance with the guidelines of the Government of India (animal facility CPCSEA registration number 109/1999/CPCSEA) and equivalent guidelines of the Society for Neuroscience.
evidence: This is a statement about ethical approval for the study.

claim: All recordings and behavioral experiments were carried out on male, 30 to 45 day old C57BL/6 mice.
source: All recordings and behavioral experiments were carried out on male, 30 to 45 day old C57BL/6 mice.
evidence: This is a description of the experimental subjects.

claim: Data acquired from a total of 35 mice is included in the study.
source: Data acquired from a total of 35 mice is included here.
evidence: This is a statement about the sample size.

claim: 18 mice were trace conditioned and 17 mice were pseudo-conditioned.
source: A total of 18 mice were trace conditioned, and 17 mice pseudo-conditioned.
evidence: This is a description of the experimental groups.

claim: Of the 18 trace conditioned mice, 9 learned the task to criterion and 9 failed to learn.
source: Of the 18 trace conditioned mice, 9 learned the task to criterion and the other 9 failed to learn.
evidence: This is a description of the behavioral outcomes.

claim: Imaging data was acquired for 14 of the trace conditioned mice, of which 6 were learners and 8 were non-learners.
source: Imaging data was acquired for 14 of the trace conditioned mice. Of these, 6 were learners and 8 were non-learners.
evidence: This is a description of the imaging dataset.

claim: Imaging data was acquired for 6 pseudo-conditioned mice.
source: Of the 17 pseudo-conditioned mice, imaging data was acquired for 6 mice (Figure 2—figure supplement 1B).
evidence: This is a description of the imaging dataset shown in Figure 2—figure supplement 1B.

claim: OGB-1 dye allows imaging for a limited period before clearance from neurons, limiting the viability of the imaging preparation to a few hours.
source: OGB-1 dye, once loaded into neurons, allows imaging for a limited period before clearance from neurons (Stosiek et al., 2003). This limited the viability of the imaging preparation to a few hours, corresponding to a single behavioral session.
evidence: This is a statement about the technical limitations of the imaging method, supported by citation.
